notes: Lennox Lewis satellite litigation; Peter Smith J finds Panos Eliades beneficial owner of Enfield property registered to deceased nominee.

enrichment.short_title: Lewis v Eliades: beneficial ownership of property registered to deceased nominee
key_facts: Mr Lennox Lewis sued his former promoter Panos Eliades and administrators of the estate of Aristos Kaissides over beneficial ownership of 39 Beech Hill, Enfield.
The property was registered in Mr Kaissides' name but formed part of wider satellite litigation arising from US proceedings over Mr Eliades' disclosed assets.
Mr Kaissides, a retired Cypriot bank manager who died intestate in 2000, could not plausibly have funded the purchase from his own means.
Mr Eliades' evidence and supporting documentation were inadequate and key witnesses did not give live evidence.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Trial in the Chancery Division on beneficial ownership of registered land in satellite litigation between Mr Lewis and Mr Eliades.
enrichment.outcome: Mr Lewis succeeded; the court held Mr Kaissides was not the beneficial owner and Mr Panos Eliades was the true beneficial owner of the property.
enrichment.ratio: Where registered land is held by a nominee, the presumption that beneficial ownership follows legal title may be rebutted on the balance of probabilities; absent any other identified candidate, the claimant need not disprove hypothetical beneficial owners but may establish the person best supported by the evidence.
legal_issues: Whether the presumption of beneficial ownership in the registered proprietor was rebutted
Whether Mr Lewis had to disprove all hypothetical beneficial owners or only establish Mr Eliades as the best candidate
What inference should be drawn from absent witnesses and missing documentation
Whether Mr Kaissides could realistically have funded the purchase
linked_authorities: Wisniewski v Central Manchester Health Authority [1998] PIQR 324
Thompson v Bryant Northern Homes [2002] EWCA Civ 1079
Rock Nominees Ltd v RCO (Holdings) PLC [2003] EWHC 936 (Ch)

confidence.notes: Final findings on beneficial ownership and reasoning on evidence are clearly recorded.

notes: Case management in combined probate and Inheritance Act proceedings; counterclaim on 2003 will to proceed to short trial.

enrichment.short_title: Green v Briscoe: probate validity and Inheritance Act claim case management

statutes_considered.title: Inheritance (Provision for Family and Dependants) Act 1975

key_facts: Mrs Green brought a claim for reasonable financial provision from the estate of Jack Green and to set aside her transfer of 186 Anerley Road for undue influence.
A separate probate claim challenged the validity of Mr Green's November 2003 will.
The defendant sought to strike out the Inheritance Act claim on the basis Mrs Green lacked standing if intestacy beneficiaries succeeded on the will challenge.
Attesting witness statements raised a real issue as to the execution of the 2003 will.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Case management hearing before Master Bragge in concurrent probate and Inheritance Act proceedings.
enrichment.outcome: The Inheritance Act claim was not struck out or discontinued; the probate counterclaim was ordered to trial on attesting witness evidence in the existing trial window.
enrichment.ratio: In concurrent probate and family provision proceedings, the court may require determination of entitlement to the estate before or alongside the 1975 Act claim; where attesting witness evidence raises a real issue on will validity, justice requires adjudication rather than discontinuance of the probate counterclaim.
legal_issues: Whether Mrs Green had sufficient interest to pursue the Inheritance Act claim
Whether the Inheritance Act claim should be struck out pending probate determination
Whether the probate counterclaim should be discontinued
How CPR 57.11 applies to discontinuance of probate claims

confidence.notes: Interlocutory case management only; substantive probate and provision issues remain for trial.

notes: Adverse possession appeal partly allowed on tape-fence interruption; deed of surrender also affected costs.

enrichment.short_title: Generay v CSC: adverse possession of Wembley trading estate strip
key_facts: Generay claimed title by adverse possession to a long narrow strip on the Wembley Stadium Trading Estate registered to Containerised Storage Company Ltd.
The county court held Generay had acquired title after about 12 years' possession, subject to boundary disputes including a 'notch' area.
During litigation Generay erected a temporary tape fence excluding part of the strip, later replaced by a more permanent fence.
CSC appealed on abandonment, the deed of surrender and interruption of possession.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal from a Central London County Court adverse possession judgment.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed only on the tape-fence point; Generay lost adverse possession of part of the strip along the notch; CSC ordered to pay 50% of appeal costs and 75% of trial costs; damages remitted.
enrichment.ratio: A temporary litigation fence does not amount to abandonment of possession, but once a more permanent fence excluded part of the strip the claimant could not continue to possess that area; failure to recognise the effect of a deed of surrender may affect costs even where title is otherwise established.
legal_issues: Whether Generay had 12 years' uninterrupted adverse possession of the strip
Whether the temporary tape fence interrupted possession
Whether a permanent fence thereafter excluded part of the strip from possession
Appropriate costs consequences where a deed of surrender was overlooked

confidence.notes: Appellate disposition on possession and costs is explicit though damages were remitted.

notes: Section 6(2) reference application dismissed; no fairly arguable point of law on agricultural holding counter-notice.

enrichment.short_title: William Smith v Parisride: section 6 reference on agricultural holding notice
key_facts: The landlord owned White House Farm, Staintondale and served notice to quit on tenant Parisride Ltd.
The tenant served a counter-notice and also referred the dispute to arbitration in the same envelope.
The Agricultural Land Tribunal upheld a preliminary point that the counter-notice was ineffective because the tenant had pursued arbitration.
The landlord applied under section 6(2) requiring the Tribunal to refer questions of law to the High Court.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court application under section 6(2) of the 1954 Act following an Agricultural Land Tribunal hearing on a notice to quit at White House Farm.
enrichment.outcome: Application dismissed; neither question of law referred by the landlord raised a fairly arguable point of law.
enrichment.ratio: A section 6(2) reference requires questions of law that are fairly arguable; where a tenant's counter-notice was rendered ineffective by pursuing arbitration under the statutory scheme, the landlord cannot obtain a High Court reference simply because it disputes the Tribunal's interpretation.
legal_issues: Whether the tenant served an effective counter-notice under section 26 of the 1986 Act
Whether a tenant may pursue arbitration and Tribunal proceedings simultaneously
Whether section 28(4)(a) invalidated the counter-notice
Whether the proposed questions of law were fairly arguable for a section 6 reference

confidence.notes: Final dismissal and reasoning on arguability are clearly stated though legislative background is complex.

notes: River Orinoco collision; Global Mariner held solely at fault for colliding with anchored Atlantic Crusader.

enrichment.short_title: Global Mariner v Atlantic Crusader: collision liability in River Orinoco
key_facts: The laden cargo vessel Global Mariner collided with the anchored Atlantic Crusader in the River Orinoco off Matanzas, Venezuela in August 2000.
Global Mariner sank within minutes though there was no loss of life.
The defendants contended Atlantic Crusader dragged anchor and failed to control yaw and sway.
Witness evidence from local tug masters was found unreliable and inconsistent with contemporaneous statements.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Admiralty collision trial in the Commercial Court on fault and apportionment.
enrichment.outcome: Global Mariner held solely to blame; no apportionment ordered; had apportionment arisen liability would have been 90% to GM and 10% to AC.
enrichment.ratio: A vessel under way which collides in daylight with a clearly visible anchored vessel following poor appreciation, lookout and turn execution bears sole responsibility; unreliable oral evidence unsupported by contemporaneous accounts may be rejected even where anchor-dragging is alleged.
legal_issues: Whether Atlantic Crusader's anchorage position was unsafe
Whether AC dragged anchor across the river
Whether AC failed to control yaw and sway
Apportionment of fault between the colliding vessels

confidence.notes: Detailed fact findings and clear sole-fault conclusion on liability.

notes: Beckham Tabloid Tales copyright claim dismissed; fair dealing for criticism/review under section 30 upheld.

enrichment.short_title: Fraser-Woodward v BBC: fair dealing over Beckham photographs
key_facts: Fraser-Woodward owned copyright in tabloid photographs of the Beckham family used in the BBC programme Tabloid Tales.
The BBC and Brighter Pictures defended on fair dealing for criticism or review and incidental inclusion.
The programme criticised celebrity tabloid journalism and used the photographs to illustrate that style of reporting.
Consent to use the photographs had been sought and refused before broadcast.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Chancery trial of a copyright infringement claim concerning use of photographs in a television documentary.
enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed; use of the first 13 photographs was fair dealing for criticism or review; no additional damages would have been awarded.
enrichment.ratio: Use of copyright photographs in a television programme may constitute fair dealing for criticism or review where the work criticises a genre of tabloid celebrity journalism rather than each specific photograph; following Pro Sieben, the criticised works need not all be individually identified if the genre is sufficiently identified.
legal_issues: Whether the programme used the photographs for criticism or review within section 30(1)
Whether the Beckham 14 photograph fell within fair dealing
Whether incidental inclusion under section 31(1) applied
Whether additional damages for flagrancy were warranted
linked_authorities: Pro Sieben Media AG v Carlton UK Television Ltd [1999] 1 WLR 605

confidence.notes: Detailed analysis of fair dealing and a clear final dismissal.

notes: Lloyd's TOBA inspection dispute; clause 8.1.2 entitlement analysed and clause 2.2 may limit placing file access.

enrichment.short_title: Goshawk v Tyser: Lloyd's TOBA document inspection rights
key_facts: Lloyd's syndicates sought inspection and copying of placing files, claims files and premium accounting documents from their brokers Tyser & Co.
The dispute arose from viatical and seniors life assurance business placed through brokers including Kalmanson-related placements.
The parties' Terms of Business Agreement included clause 8.1.2 granting managing agents inspection rights and clause 2.2 prioritising client interests.
Brokers feared production would prejudice clients and expose them to claims long after placement.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Commercial Court trial of preliminary issues on brokers' obligation to permit document inspection under Lloyd's TOBA terms.
enrichment.outcome: The court analysed TOBA clause 8.1.2 and held syndicates were entitled to defined documentation subject to clause 2.2; brokers had genuine grounds to refuse placing and claims files but not premium accounting documents on present material.
enrichment.ratio: Under a Lloyd's TOBA, clause 8.1.2 gives managing agents a contractual entitlement to inspect disclosed placing and claims documentation in the brokers' possession, but clause 2.2 may override that entitlement where the broker genuinely considers access contrary to the client's interests.
legal_issues: Whether an implied or customary right of inspection existed outside the TOBA
Construction of TOBA clause 8.1.2 and the documents it covers
Whether clause 2.2 qualifies or overrides inspection rights
Whether syndicates could use CPR disclosure as a shortcut before formulating complaints

confidence.notes: Detailed contractual analysis though some document categories were addressed provisionally pending further order.

notes: Long-running possession litigation; Court of Appeal refuses adjournment and directs CPR 52.17 as only route.

enrichment.short_title: Messer v Messer: jurisdiction to reopen final possession appeal
key_facts: Mrs Messer had been ordered in 2000 to give up possession of property in Old Harlow and was eventually evicted in March 2005.
The possession order was finally determined when permission to appeal was refused in July 2004.
She sought to reopen proceedings and set aside the possession order, relying on lack of understanding and need for legal assistance.
Parallel litigation concerned a suspended committal order for contempt.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application to the Court of Appeal to adjourn and reopen final possession and committal orders after eviction.
enrichment.outcome: Applications for adjournment and to set aside refused; the court held it had no jurisdiction to reopen the final possession determination except on a written application under CPR 52.17.
enrichment.ratio: Once a possession order and related appeal process are finally determined, the Court of Appeal cannot entertain a fresh challenge to the possession order except under the strict criteria in CPR 52.17; an adjournment serves no purpose where the application outside Rule 52.17 is bound to fail.
legal_issues: Whether the Court of Appeal could set aside the final possession order
Whether CPR 52.17 was the only remaining route to reopen the appeal
Whether an adjournment should be granted to allow further applications
Relationship between committal proceedings and the underlying possession order

confidence.notes: Jurisdictional ruling and final refusal are clearly reasoned.

notes: Section 13 coroner appeal; new inquest ordered after new pupil evidence on school hanging death.

enrichment.short_title: Parkin v coroner: fresh inquest after school death of Bradley Parkin
key_facts: Bradley Parkin, aged 17, was found hanging in a school props room at Lindsey School, Cleethorpes in February 2000.
The coroner returned an open verdict after an inquest hearing limited pupil evidence.
Mrs Parkin appealed under section 13 and obtained new statements from pupils not called at the original inquest.
The death predated the Human Rights Act but the inquest occurred afterwards.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal under section 13 of the Coroners Act 1988 against an open verdict following an inquest into a school death.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; a fresh inquest ordered before a different coroner on the basis of insufficiency of inquiry and new evidence.
enrichment.ratio: Under section 13(1)(b) a fresh inquest may be ordered where new evidence makes it necessary or desirable in the interests of justice; following In re Rapier it is sufficient that a different verdict is possible, not that it is probable.
legal_issues: Whether Article 2 investigative standards applied to a pre-HRA death
Whether the original inquest was insufficient in scope
Whether newly obtained pupil statements justified a fresh inquest
The test for quashing an inquest under section 13
linked_authorities: R v HM Coroner for North Humberside ex parte Jamieson [1995] QB 1
R (Middleton) v West Somerset Coroner [2004] 2 AC 182

confidence.notes: Appellate reasoning on section 13 and the order for a new inquest are explicit.

notes: Extradition appeal to Australia; rehearing ordered for expert evidence on Article 6 and Australian burden of proof.

enrichment.short_title: Okendeji v Australia: Article 6 rehearing on extradition fair trial
key_facts: Australia sought extradition of Nigerian national Okendeji for alleged cocaine importation and failure to surrender to bail.
The appellant argued extradition would involve a flagrant breach of Article 6 because Australian drug importation provisions reversed the legal burden of proof.
The District Judge dismissed the human rights challenge without expert evidence on Australian law.
An entrapment argument was rejected on affidavit evidence from the Australian Federal Police.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal under section 103 of the Extradition Act 2003 against a district judge's extradition order to Australia.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal not finally decided on Article 6 merits; the court directed a rehearing before the District Judge with expert evidence on Australian law including burden of proof and 'without reasonable excuse'.
enrichment.ratio: Where extradition is resisted on the basis of foreign law engaging Article 6, the requesting state must meet the issue with expert evidence; a district judge should adjourn rather than dismiss when notified of a live foreign-law point, and 'flagrant denial' of fair trial must be given real meaning and not equated with any Article 6 breach.
legal_issues: Whether Australian customs provisions imposed a legal or evidential burden of proof
Whether extradition would involve a flagrant denial of Article 6 rights
Whether the District Judge should have adjourned for expert evidence on Australian law
Whether state-endorsed entrapment rendered extradition an abuse of process
linked_authorities: Elliot v United Kingdom (2003) Application no. 35794/97

confidence.notes: Rehearing direction is clear though final Article 6 outcome was expressly deferred.
